name: Ready-to-eat grains and crackers
role: Carbohydrate energy that can be eaten when cooking water or fuel is unavailable.
examples: Oat or grain bars suited to household allergies
unopenedLife: Ready-to-eat cereal: about 6–12 months for best quality in a cool, dry pantry. Crackers and bars follow their own package dates; this is not a safety expiration.
afterOpening: Dry cereal: about 2–3 months for quality when resealed; other products follow the label. Once mixed with milk or other wet ingredients, the mixture becomes perishable.
storage: Keep dry, cool and protected from pests in a closed food-safe container. Retain the original label and allergen information.
waterFuel: No cooking water or fuel for products labeled ready to eat. Drinking water is still needed; dry food is not a substitute for water.
notes: Keep several familiar no-cook meals. Choose portions people will actually eat and check wheat, milk, soy and nut ingredients.

name: Quick-cooking dry starches
role: Affordable meal calories; select quick-cooking versions to reduce time at the burner.
unopenedLife: Approximate pantry quality examples: dry pasta 24 months; plain white rice 24 months; brown rice 12 months; oatmeal 6–12 months. Instant grains, blends and pouches follow their specific labels; these are not safety deadlines.
afterOpening: Keep the dry food sealed and dry. Cooked rice, pasta, oats and other moist starches require prompt chilling; without refrigeration, make only the current meal.
storage: Use a pest-resistant container in a dry cupboard, away from cleaning chemicals and heat.
waterFuel: Needs measured potable water and the package cooking time. Prefer absorption recipes; draining a large pot wastes water. Instant does not automatically mean safe to eat dry or cold-soak.
notes: Read directions before buying. A dry-grain stock without enough cooking water and suitable fuel is incomplete. Include ready-to-eat grains as backup.

name: Canned beans, peas and lentils
role: Plant protein, fiber and useful meal calories without a long boil.
unopenedLife: Commercial low-acid cans: about 2–5 years for best quality under suitable storage. This is a rotation guide, not a safety guarantee or a required wait.
afterOpening: Refrigerate unused beans promptly. Without refrigeration, use a meal-sized can and discard unused contents after 2 hours, or 1 hour above 90°F/32°C; never save overnight.
storage: Keep cans dry and cool; rotate older stock forward. Reject leaking, swollen or deeply dented cans, including dents affecting seams.
waterFuel: Fully cooked ready-to-eat beans need no further cooking. Lower-sodium products can avoid a rinse when water is scarce; their liquid can thin a hot dish.
notes: Dry beans have different preparation and fuel needs. Do not substitute uncooked dry beans directly into a canned-bean recipe.

name: Shelf-stable canned fish, poultry or meat
role: Concentrated protein; canned fish with edible bones can also contribute calcium.
unopenedLife: Low-acid commercial cans: about 2–5 years for best quality. Pouches and special products follow their own label; not every canned meat is shelf-stable.
afterOpening: Opened meat and fish are perishable. Refrigerate promptly; without refrigeration, discard unused contents after 2 hours, or 1 hour above 90°F/32°C. Choose a meal-sized container.
storage: Buy only products explicitly suitable for room-temperature storage. A 'keep refrigerated' ham is not pantry food. Protect cans and pouches from damage.
waterFuel: No water or fuel for products labeled fully cooked and ready to eat. Empty into cookware if warming; never heat a sealed can or pouch.
notes: Check fish and other allergens, serving sizes and sodium. Choose fish species and quantities appropriate for pregnancy and children using current FDA/EPA fish advice.

name: Shelf-stable nut or seed butters
role: Compact calories, fat and some protein for no-cook meals.
unopenedLife: Commercial peanut butter: about 6–9 months for best quality in a cool pantry. Other nut/seed butters and natural formulations follow their own labels; this is not a safety expiration.
afterOpening: Typical shelf-stable peanut butter: about 2–3 months for quality. Some natural spreads require refrigeration after opening; follow the label or choose single portions for a no-fridge plan.
storage: Keep tightly closed, away from heat; use a clean, dry utensil and prevent crumbs or water entering the jar.
waterFuel: No cooking water or fuel. Spread on crackers or stir into cooked meals; reserve drinking water separately.
notes: Check peanut, tree-nut, sesame and seed allergies. This is not an infant feeding plan; choose age-appropriate foods and textures.

name: Cooking oils
role: Adds energy and fat to otherwise lean grain and bean meals.
unopenedLife: Vegetable or olive oil: about 6–12 months for best quality in a cool, dark pantry. Packaging and oil type vary; follow the product date rather than treating this as a safety expiration.
afterOpening: About 3–5 months for quality for typical vegetable/olive oil stored suitably; recap and follow the label. Keep water and food debris out and rotate a small bottle through normal cooking.
storage: Keep in its closed, labeled food container in a cool, dark cupboard, away from the burner and from fuel containers.
waterFuel: No water or fuel to add oil to a meal. A little can reduce sticking; deep-frying uses much more oil and creates additional fire and disposal problems.
notes: Rotate through normal cooking. Oil is food, not approved stove fuel. Rancid oil has lost quality; an unexpired date does not protect a badly stored product.

name: Canned vegetables and tomatoes
role: Vegetable variety, fiber and micronutrients alongside calorie and protein staples.
unopenedLife: Low-acid vegetable cans: about 2–5 years for best quality; high-acid tomatoes: about 12–18 months. Check the actual product label.
afterOpening: Refrigerate unused contents. Without cold storage, use a meal-sized can and discard unused opened food after 2 hours, or 1 hour above 90°F/32°C; do not keep it overnight.
storage: Keep cans out of damp or hot locations. Reject damaged seals, leaking, bulging or badly dented cans; never taste suspect food.
waterFuel: Ready-to-eat commercial products can be served cold. Use suitable packing liquid in soup instead of automatically draining and adding fresh water.
notes: Choose lower-sodium options where available. Canned vegetables complement a pantry but do not replace sufficient calories, protein, fat or drinking water.

name: Canned fruit and unsweetened fruit cups
role: Ready-to-eat fruit variety and a familiar food when fresh produce is unavailable.
unopenedLife: High-acid commercial fruit cans: about 12–18 months for best quality. Plastic cups, pouches and applesauce follow their own label.
afterOpening: Follow the product's refrigeration instructions after opening. Individual cups avoid planning for an opened container when no refrigerator is available.
storage: Protect cups and pouches from punctures and cans from rust or dents; keep dry, cool and away from direct sunlight.
waterFuel: No cooking water or fuel for ready-to-eat products. Juice can moisten porridge; do not count canned juice as the entire drinking-water supply.
notes: Choose fruit the household tolerates. Best-quality dates do not overrule package damage, recalls or unsafe storage.

name: Shelf-stable milk or fortified soy beverage
role: A practical calcium source; milk and fortified soy beverages can also add protein. Read nutrient labels.
examples: Shelf-stable calcium- and vitamin-D-fortified soy beverage
Nonfat dry milk prepared exactly as directed
unopenedLife: Aseptically packaged shelf-stable UHT milk: roughly 6 months as a planning example; exact product dates govern. Fortified soy beverages and milk powder follow their own labels. Refrigerated ultra-pasteurized cartons are not automatically shelf-stable.
afterOpening: Opened milk/soy beverage and reconstituted milk require refrigeration. Without it, use a single portion now and discard after 2 hours, or 1 hour above 90°F/32°C. Dry powder follows its label.
storage: Keep unopened shelf-stable cartons cool and undamaged. Keep milk powder dry and tightly sealed; use clean measuring equipment.
waterFuel: UHT cartons need no added water or heat. Powder requires the label's measured amount of potable water; reconstitution does not create shelf-stable liquid milk.
notes: Plant beverages differ in protein, calcium and vitamin D. Milk, soy and other allergies matter. These drinks are not infant formula; use an infant-specific feeding plan when needed.

name: Dry beans, lentils and split peas
role: Inexpensive plant protein for households with dependable cooking water, time and fuel.
examples: Dry beans with package preparation instructions
unopenedLife: Dry beans: about 12–24 months for best quality in ordinary pantry storage. Lentils and split peas follow their labels. Older pulses may soften slowly; this is not a safety expiration.
afterOpening: Keep dry pulses sealed against moisture and pests. Cooked pulses are perishable and require chilling if not eaten promptly.
storage: Store dry in a labeled, food-safe pest-resistant container, retaining the preparation directions.
waterFuel: Needs more water and usually more burner time than canned pulses. Follow soaking and boiling directions; do not rely on cold soaking or a brief warm-up to cook raw beans.
notes: Build the low-water, no-cook supply first. Dry kidney beans especially require correct preparation; these stove recipes use commercially cooked beans instead.

name: Nuts and seeds
role: Portable fats, some protein and extra meal calories.
unopenedLife: Commercial unopened packaged nut meats: up to about 12 months as a quality example; pine nuts can be much shorter, about 2–3 weeks in the pantry. Exact packaging and label govern; do not generalize to every nut or seed.
afterOpening: Reseal and follow the label. For ordinary shelled nuts, a conservative room-temperature quality window is about 2–4 weeks; refrigeration preserves quality longer. Prefer small packs without a refrigerator.
storage: Keep cool, dry, dark and sealed. Protect from pests and avoid carrying loose nuts beside fuel or chemicals.
waterFuel: No cooking water or fuel for products sold ready to eat.
notes: Check allergies and age-appropriate choking precautions. Choose unsalted products when possible; snacks supplement complete meals.

name: Dried fruit and dehydrated vegetables
role: Lightweight produce variety; dried fruit is an easy no-cook addition.
unopenedLife: Dried fruit: about 6 months for best quality in a cool, dry pantry. Commercial dehydrated vegetables and special sealed packs follow their own labels; this is not a safety expiration.
afterOpening: Ordinary dried fruit: about 1 month for pantry quality; reseal and obey any refrigeration instruction. Rehydrated dishes should be eaten at the current meal or chilled.
storage: Keep moisture out and inspect packaging for pest damage. Retain any instructions requiring cooking or refrigeration.
waterFuel: Ready-to-eat dried fruit needs no cooking. Dehydrated vegetables may require measured potable water and boiling; reserve both before choosing them over cans.
notes: Do not assume all freeze-dried or dehydrated foods are ready to eat. Follow preparation instructions and check sulfite declarations if relevant.

name: Canned soups and complete meals
role: Convenient familiar meals when attention, equipment or preparation time is limited.
unopenedLife: Low-acid commercial canned meals often use a 2–5-year best-quality window; acidic tomato products can be shorter. The exact product label governs rotation.
afterOpening: Refrigerate unused soup or meal promptly. Without refrigeration, discard unused contents after 2 hours, or 1 hour above 90°F/32°C; open only enough for the current meal.
storage: Keep cool and dry; inspect seals and rotate stock. Avoid relying on glass containers where breakage is likely.
waterFuel: Ready-to-serve products need no added water. Condensed soups need label-specified liquid. Warm only in proper cookware, never in a sealed can.
notes: Read calories, protein and sodium per entire container; a 'meal' name does not mean it meets a person's whole-day needs.

name: Seasonings and small condiment portions
role: Makes repeated pantry meals palatable without needing many additional ingredients.
examples: Bouillon appropriate for the household diet
unopenedLife: Pantry quality examples: dried herbs about 1–2 years; bouillon cubes/granules about 1 year. Sauces and single-use packets follow their own label dates; these are not safety expirations.
afterOpening: Keep dry seasonings dry. Follow sauce refrigeration directions; single-use packets avoid an opened bottle that needs chilling.
storage: Keep sealed, labeled and away from heat. Do not transfer food into containers that previously held non-food substances.
waterFuel: Dry seasoning uses no extra fuel. Bouillon is flavoring, not drinking water or a complete meal; reconstitute only with potable water.
notes: Choose mild, lower-sodium options where useful. Large amounts of salty foods increase thirst; check wheat, soy, sesame and other allergens.

name: Tea, coffee and other comfort drinks
role: Familiar routines and morale after the core food and water supply is covered.
examples: Cocoa mix suited to household allergies
unopenedLife: Instant coffee: about 1 year; tea bags: about 18–36 months, as pantry quality examples. Cocoa/milk-containing mixes follow their own dates. These are not safety expirations.
afterOpening: Instant coffee: about 2–3 months for quality when tightly resealed. Keep other dry mixes and scoops dry and follow their labels. Prepared milk-containing drinks are perishable; make only what will be consumed.
storage: Keep dry in a closed container away from strong odors and cooking fuel.
waterFuel: A hot drink uses potable water and additional burner time. Cold preparation is appropriate only where the product directions allow it.
notes: Optional comfort items should not displace meals, safe water or essential dietary supplies. Check caffeine preferences and milk/soy ingredients.
